## Independence

### Basic Definitions

::: {#def-aap-2-1 name="Independent Events"}

Two events $A$ and $B$ are **independent** if

$$
P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B).
$$

:::

::: {#def-aap-2-2 name="Independent Random Variables"}

Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables defined on the same
probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$:

$$
X,Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(\mathbb R,\mathcal R).
$$

They are **independent** if, for all $C,D\in\mathcal R$,

$$
P(X\in C,Y\in D)=P(X\in C)P(Y\in D).
$$

That is, the events $A=\{X\in C\}$ and $B=\{Y\in D\}$ are independent.

:::

::: {#def-aap-2-3 name="Independent σ-Fields"}

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal H,P)$ be a probability space, and let
$\mathcal F,\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal H$ be two sub-$\sigma$-fields. They are
**independent** if

$$
P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B),
\qquad\forall A\in\mathcal F,\ \forall B\in\mathcal G.
$$

That is, every event in $\mathcal F$ is independent of every event in $\mathcal G$.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-2-1 name="Independence and Generated σ-Fields"}

Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables on the same probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal H,P)$.

i) If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $\sigma(X)$ and $\sigma(Y)$ are independent.

ii) Conversely, if $\mathcal F,\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal H$ are independent
    sub-$\sigma$-fields, $X$ is $\mathcal F$-measurable, and $Y$ is
    $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

:::

### Independence of Finite Families

Work on a common probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal H,P)$.

::: {#def-aap-2-4 name="Independence of Finitely Many σ-Fields"}

The sub-$\sigma$-fields
$\mathcal F_1,\ldots,\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal H$ are **independent** if,
whenever $A_i\in\mathcal F_i$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$,

$$
P\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n A_i\right)=\prod_{i=1}^n P(A_i).
$$

:::

::: {#def-aap-2-5 name="Independence of Finitely Many Random Variables"}

The random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are **independent**
if, whenever $B_i\in\mathcal R$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$,

$$
P\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n\{X_i\in B_i\}\right)
=\prod_{i=1}^n P(X_i\in B_i).
$$

:::

::: {#def-aap-2-6 name="Independence of Finitely Many Events"}

The events $A_1,\ldots,A_n\in\mathcal H$ are **independent** if, for
every nonempty subset $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$,

$$
P\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i\right)=\prod_{i\in I}P(A_i).
$$

:::

### Joint Distributions

::: {#thm-aap-2-2 name="Joint Distribution of Independent Random Variables"}

Suppose $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent random variables and $X_i$ has
distribution $\mu_i$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$. Then $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ has distribution

$$
\mu_1\times\cdots\times\mu_n.
$$

:::

### Expectations

::: {#thm-aap-2-3 name="Expectations of Functions of Independent Random Variables"}

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are independent and have distributions $\mu$ and $\nu$.
Let $h:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. If either

a) $h\ge0$, or

b) $E|h(X,Y)|<\infty$,

then

$$
E[h(X,Y)]=\iint_{\mathbb R^2}h(x,y)\,\mu(dx)\,\nu(dy).
$$

In particular, let $h(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$, where $f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ are
measurable functions. If either

a) $f,g\ge0$, or

b) both $E|f(X)|<\infty$ and $E|g(Y)|<\infty$,

then

$$
E[f(X)g(Y)]=E[f(X)]\cdot E[g(Y)].
$$

:::

::: {#thm-aap-2-4 name="Expectation of a Product of Independent Random Variables"}

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent random variables. If either

a) $X_i\ge0$ for all $i$, or

b) $E|X_i|<\infty$ for all $i$,

then

$$
E\left[\prod_{i=1}^n X_i\right]=\prod_{i=1}^n EX_i.
$$

:::

### Sums and Convolution

::: {#thm-aap-2-5 name="Distribution of the Sum of Independent Random Variables"}

If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, $F(x)=P(X\le x)$, and $G(y)=P(Y\le y)$,
then

$$
P(X+Y\le z)=\int_{\mathbb R}F(z-y)\,dG(y).
$$

:::

**Convolution:** The integral on the right-hand side is called the
**convolution** of $F$ and $G$ and is denoted by $(F*G)(z)$.

Here $dG(y)$ denotes integration with respect to the distribution measure of $Y$.

## Conditional Expectation

::: {#def-aap-2-7 name="Conditional Expectation"}

Given a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F_0,P)$, a sub-$\sigma$-field
$\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal F_0$, and an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable random
variable $X$ with $E|X|<\infty$, the conditional expectation of $X$ given
$\mathcal F$, denoted $E(X\mid\mathcal F)$, is any random variable $Y$ satisfying:

i) $Y$ is $\mathcal F$-measurable.

ii) For all $A\in\mathcal F$,

    $$
    \int_A X\,dP=\int_A Y\,dP.
    $$

Any $Y$ satisfying (i) and (ii) is called a version of $E(X\mid\mathcal F)$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example: Conditioning on a Random Variable" collapse="true"}

Let $E|X|<\infty$ and $\mathcal F=\sigma(Z)$. Then

$$
Y=E[X\mid\mathcal F]=E[X\mid Z]=g(Z)\quad\text{a.s.}
$$

Here $Y$ is an $\mathcal F$-measurable **random variable**, and $g$ is measurable. Pointwise,

$$
Y(\omega)=g(Z(\omega))\quad\text{for almost every }\omega.
$$

Thus, $Y$ depends only on $Z$; observing $Z=z$ determines its value $g(z)$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Conditional Expectation as Optimal Prediction" collapse="true"}

If $E[X^2]<\infty$, $Y=E[X\mid Z]$ is the best predictor of $X$ based on $Z$ under squared loss:

$$
E[(X-Y)^2]=\min_{h\text{ measurable}}E[(X-h(Z))^2].
$$

In regression, $Z$ contains the input features and $X$ is the target; training with squared loss approximates $E[X\mid Z]$ within the chosen model class.

:::

### Regular Conditional Probabilities

::: {#def-aap-2-8 name="Regular Conditional Distribution"}

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space,
$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\mathcal S)$ a measurable map, and
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-$\sigma$-field. A map
$\mu:\Omega\times\mathcal S\to[0,1]$ is a regular conditional distribution
for $X$ given $\mathcal G$ if:

i) For each $A\in\mathcal S$, $\omega\mapsto\mu(\omega,A)$ is a version of
   $P(X\in A\mid\mathcal G)$.

ii) For almost every $\omega$, $A\mapsto\mu(\omega,A)$ is a probability
    measure on $(S,\mathcal S)$.

When $S=\Omega$ and $X$ is the identity map, $\mu$ is called a regular
conditional probability.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example: Conditional Distribution from a Joint Density" collapse="true"}

Suppose $X,Y$ have a joint density $f(x,y)>0$. For Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, define

$$
\mu(y,A)=\frac{\displaystyle\int_A f(x,y)\,dx}
{\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb R}f(x,y)\,dx}.
$$

Where the denominator is not finite and positive, choose any fixed probability distribution instead.

Then $(\omega,A)\mapsto\mu(Y(\omega),A)$ is a **regular conditional distribution** of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$: $\mu(y,\cdot)$ gives the distribution of $X$ after observing $Y=y$.

:::

## Supplementary Notes {.supplementary-notes}

### Key Results

- @thm-aap-2-1: Independent random variables generate independent $\sigma$-fields, and variables measurable with respect to independent $\sigma$-fields are independent.
- @thm-aap-2-2: Independent random variables have the product distribution $\mu_1\times\cdots\times\mu_n$ as their joint distribution.
- @thm-aap-2-3 and @thm-aap-2-4: Under independence, $E[f(X)g(Y)]=E[f(X)]\cdot E[g(Y)]$, and expectation factors over products.
- @thm-aap-2-5: $P(X+Y\le z)=\int_{\mathbb R}F(z-y)\,dG(y)$, the convolution of $F$ and $G$.
- @def-aap-2-7: $E(X\mid\mathcal F)$ is an $\mathcal F$-measurable variable with the same integral as $X$ over every $A\in\mathcal F$.
